title: Assisted performance: Gains vary by skill measure
desc: Separates speed, quality, activity and AI agreement, rejecting automatic equalization or worker substitution from team-level results.

kps.k: AI assistance produces task-specific gains, not a uniform improvement in performance or an automatic narrowing of skill gaps.
kps.d: The cluster contributes empirical evidence to the debate over whether AI substitutes for existing skills or complements them. Writing coaching, image identification and technical support show gains on identifiable outcomes; the Kenya entrepreneurship experiment finds no significant average performance gain, and the radiology experiment finds greater agreement with AI without clear improvement against the diagnostic standard. These differences concern distinct tasks, interventions and populations, rather than a direct dispute between studies estimating the same effect.

qs.q: As shown in Column I of Table 3, the coefficient of AI is positive and statistically significant (β = 0.239, p < 0.01), indicating that students with access to the AI assistant achieve a substantially higher score gain compared to those in the control group.
qs.a: Does AI Equalize or Amplify? Evidence from Two Field Experiments in AI-powered Learning · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Column 1 shows the impact of AI assistance on accuracy in a simple bivariation regression.9 AI improves participants’ ability to accurately identify an image by 6.9 percentage points, an increase of more than 10 percent relative to the control mean of 65.5 percent.
qs.a: The ABC's of Who Benefits from Working with AI: Ability, Beliefs, and Calibration · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The distribution of benefits depends on which dimension of skill the study measures.
kps.d: In Kenya, one adjusted completed-panel specification estimates −0.088 standard deviations for initially lower-performing entrepreneurs and +0.190 for higher performers, with a significant 0.267 differential; the higher-performer gain itself meets only the 10% threshold. The writing-coaching experiment also finds larger gains for students with higher baseline scores. By contrast, the image-identification study reports smaller assistance gains at higher baseline accuracy and IQ, but larger gains with better calibration. The education-gap experiment finds no significant treatment-effect difference across education groups on follow-up scores. Baseline performance, education, IQ and calibration therefore cannot stand in for one common measure of expertise.

qs.a: The Uneven Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Entrepreneurial Performance: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Kenya · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Speed, activity, quality and agreement with AI measure different consequences of deployment.
kps.d: Generative AI at Work estimates faster handling and greater hourly throughput, but only weak evidence of improved resolution rates and no significant customer-satisfaction change. In radiology, judgments move toward AI predictions while changes against the diagnostic standard remain near zero; measured effort does not uniformly fall. Generative AI and the Nature of Work reports that Copilot eligibility increased coding activity by 9.0–12.4% and reduced project-management activity by 20.1–24.9% during July 2022–July 2023. That finding establishes a change in recorded work activities, not a corresponding improvement in output quality or a reduction in employment.

qs.q: Post AI X Treated measures the impact of AI model deployment after deployment on treated agents for average handle time or average      call duration, chats per hour, the number of chats an agent handles per hour, resolution rate, the share of technical support problems they can resolve and net      promoter score (NPS), an estimate of customer satisfaction, and each metrics corresponding natural log equivalents.

kps.k: Team and firm results do not by themselves establish substitution for workers.
kps.d: The Cybernetic Teammate reports higher standardized solution quality for AI-assisted individuals and teams relative to the reference group. However, direct comparisons do not establish that AI-assisted teams outperform unaided teams on average quality or top-decile outcomes at the 5% level. Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market reports positive firm-level IV coefficients for sales, employment, profits and total factor productivity across identifiable robustness specifications. Those firm-level results differ from task-level productivity evidence and do not establish economy-wide employment effects.

kps.k: Interaction design and user behavior may matter, but the evidence distinguishes tested interventions from proposed mechanisms.
kps.d: The learning experiment finds that disclosure and feedback can improve score gains and engagement without significantly increasing measured AI usage; feedback estimates use a sample restricted to positive AI users. Its authors attribute writing gains to immediate diagnostic feedback and modular guidance, but the supplied material does not separately demonstrate that mechanism. The education-gap experiment links detailed instructions, iterative engagement and structured workflows to higher scores through observational regressions, not randomized tests of those practices. Kenya's non-preregistered text analysis likewise does not establish that particular advice caused profit gains.

qs.q: Panel B is restricted to      observations with positive AI use, following the original specification.

qs.q: That is, AI-enabled learning improves writing performance by providing immediate diagnostic feedback and modularized guidance during the writing process.

kps.k: The judicial evidence concerns adoption and attitudes, not demonstrated gains in adjudication.
kps.d: Courts of Tomorrow finds no significant difference between targeted and generic training in regular self-reported AI use; this does not establish equivalence, and the supplied coefficients do not establish either intervention's overall effect. More tool logins predict stronger support for generative AI, but the excerpt does not provide enough identification detail to treat that relationship as causal. These findings leave judicial productivity and decision quality unresolved in the supplied material.

qs.q: The dependent variable is an indicator equal to one if the judge reports using generative AI at least once or twice a week in the post-intervention survey, and zero otherwise.
qs.a: Courts of Tomorrow: Evidence from a Nationwide Rollout of Generative AI · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Practical interpretation requires local outcome tests and explicit limits on robustness and generalization.
kps.d: The evidence supports evaluating deployment separately by task, baseline capability, quality, effort and distribution of gains rather than relying on adoption counts or average productivity alone. Kenya's performance differential persists across several checks but loses significance under the supplied log-like transformation. Missing outcome headings prevent substantive interpretation of several taxi-driver, analyst, OECD and creativity tables; coefficient signs cannot fill those gaps. The studies also use different causal designs and skill definitions. Most do not study legal work, so they provide hypotheses for legal deployment rather than direct estimates of its effects.

qs.q: Because inequality was measured in different ways across the studies (e.g., based on experience versus pre-treatment performance), we report only qualitative conclusions about the effect on inequality.
qs.a: The Uneven Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Entrepreneurial Performance: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Kenya · Academia · 2026
Artificial Intelligence and High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Analysts · Academia · 2020

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources support the proposition that AI-assisted performance is task-, outcome- and skill-measure-specific, rather than uniformly beneficial, automatically equalising or demonstrative of worker substitution. Their common basis is empirical separation of outcomes that are often conflated: studies distinguish speed and throughput from resolution and customer satisfaction; coding activity from project-management activity and output quality; agreement with AI from diagnostic accuracy; and adoption or attitudes from demonstrated performance. They also repeatedly find heterogeneous effects, but the direction varies with the construct used: higher baseline performers benefit more in the Kenya entrepreneurship and writing-coaching studies, whereas image-identification gains decline with baseline accuracy and IQ but rise with calibration; education groups show no significant treatment-effect difference. Material internal variation includes clear average gains on some bounded tasks, insignificant average effects or adverse subgroup estimates elsewhere, and positive firm-level associations that cannot establish economy-wide substitution. Several sources are only partly interpretable because outcomes or table headings are missing, while the Kenya findings vary under an alternative outcome transformation. Thus, this selected research evidence supports the proposition through convergent methodological caution, not through a single universal effect or any claim that the sources represent academia generally.

qs.q: Because inequality was measured in different ways across the studies (e.g., based on experience versus pre-treatment performance), we report only qualitative conclusions about the effect on inequality.
qs.a: The Uneven Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Entrepreneurial Performance: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Kenya · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The OECD source supports the proposition’s central caution that AI adoption cannot be treated as evidence of uniform performance gains, skill equalisation or worker substitution. Its supplied evidence consists only of truncated regression-table fragments: outcome headings, units, definitions and explanatory notes are missing, so coefficient signs cannot identify what improved or worsened or support causal conclusions. Within the source, the trade-union and worker-council specifications show material variation: representation coefficients are mostly positive across the displayed columns, while interactions with AI adoption vary in sign and statistical significance. This reinforces the cluster’s case for outcome-specific, locally interpretable tests rather than broad conclusions from adoption measures or isolated coefficients. However, the source provides methodological support rather than direct evidence about speed, quality, activity or employment effects. As this is one curated source, its position should not be taken as representative of regulators, courts and professional bodies generally.

elens.an: The selected 2015–2022 sources support the proposition that AI-assisted performance is heterogeneous and cannot be reduced to uniform gains, automatic skill equalization or worker substitution. Both provide specification-dependent quantitative evidence rather than broad substitution claims. The taxi-driver study most directly reinforces the skill-distribution point: AI-usage coefficients differ across halves, tertiles and quartiles of measured driver skill, with more negative and more frequently statistically marked estimates among lower-skilled groups. The analyst study reinforces the need to separate outcomes and specifications: estimated associations are positive and statistically marked in some columns but near zero and unmarked in others. Material variation remains between the sources. The taxi evidence explicitly stratifies workers by skill and therefore bears directly on heterogeneous effects, although the missing outcome label prevents interpreting the direction as a productivity gain or loss. The analyst evidence concerns alternative AI-intensity definitions and accuracy thresholds, but missing outcome headings and truncated notes make its substantive relationship to skill and performance less determinate. Accordingly, these curated sources support cautious, local interpretation rather than establishing a common effect across occupations, outcomes or skill measures.

qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Analysts · Academia · 2020

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that AI-assisted performance must be assessed by specific task, skill measure and outcome rather than inferred as a uniform gain or worker substitution. The clearest evidence comes from two experiments: image-identification accuracy improves on average, but the benefit varies differently with baseline accuracy, calibration and IQ; in radiology, AI availability moves judgments toward the AI without a corresponding clear improvement against the diagnostic standard, while measured effort does not uniformly decline. Material internal variation lies in the type of support: the image-identification study demonstrates a task-specific average gain and heterogeneous treatment effects, whereas the radiology study shows that agreement with AI, diagnostic accuracy and effort can diverge. The OECD and creativity excerpts add only methodological caution because their missing outcome headings and other context make their coefficients substantively uninterpretable; another source contains too little material to classify. Thus, not every record independently establishes the proposition, but the interpretable evidence aligns with it and none clearly opposes it. Because these are curated sources, this assessment describes their relationship to the proposition and does not imply prevalence among 2023–2024 researchers or publications.

elens.an: The 2025 sources support the proposition that AI-assisted gains are outcome- and task-specific and do not, by themselves, establish skill equalization or worker substitution. Across the curated evidence, the common pattern is measurement-specific: technical-support deployment improved handling time and throughput but offered only weak evidence on resolution and none on customer satisfaction; Copilot eligibility shifted developer activity toward coding and away from project management without demonstrating better output quality or reduced employment; and AI-assisted teams recorded higher quality estimates, yet direct comparisons with unaided teams were not statistically significant at the 5% level. Firm-level robustness tests broaden the evidence by associating AI applications positively with sales, employment, profit and total factor productivity, but these aggregate relationships cannot be translated directly into uniform task-level gains or economy-wide substitution. Material internal variation therefore concerns the level and dimension measured—firm outcomes, team quality, individual workflow activity or service performance—rather than disagreement over the need for outcome-specific interpretation. Some truncated tables also lack outcome labels, reinforcing the proposition’s caution about drawing conclusions from adoption or coefficient signs alone. Because these sources are curated, their agreement should not be treated as evidence of prevalence among 2025 researchers or organisations.

The 2026 sources support the proposition that AI-assisted performance gains are task- and measure-specific, unevenly distributed, and insufficient on their own to establish either skill equalization or worker substitution. The common basis is careful separation of outcomes and populations: AI writing coaching improves scores and engagement, with larger gains among students who began with higher scores; the Kenya field experiment finds no significant average entrepreneurial-performance gain but materially different effects for initially weaker and stronger entrepreneurs; and the education experiment does not establish that treatment narrowed education-based follow-up gaps. The judicial study reinforces the distinction between adoption or attitudes and performance because its reported outcomes concern self-reported use and support for AI rather than adjudicative productivity or quality. Material variation remains. Kenya provides the strongest evidence of potentially adverse effects for lower performers, but its heterogeneity result is sensitive to the outcome transformation. The writing study finds clearer positive average gains, although its proposed feedback mechanism is interpretive rather than separately identified. The education study finds no significant differential by education group, showing that baseline score, prior performance and education are not interchangeable measures of skill. Finally, the coding excerpt is aligned methodologically with the proposition but remains inconclusive because it supplies only a pre-adoption placebo and the specification—not the results—for experience-based heterogeneity. These curated sources therefore converge on differentiated, local evaluation rather than a universal direction or size of effect, without implying that this pattern represents all 2026 research.
